claim: MemRL, a non-parametric approach that performs reinforcement learning on episodic memory with a Two-Phase Retrieval mechanism, reconciles the stability-plasticity dilemma and enables continuous runtime improvement without weight updates.
method: Decouple stable reasoning (frozen model) from plastic episodic memory, and use a Two-Phase Retrieval mechanism that filters noise and identifies high-utility strategies through environmental feedback, updating memory rather than weights.
evidence: Experiments on HLE, BigCodeBench, ALFWorld, and Lifelong Agent Bench; MemRL is said to significantly outperform state-of-the-art baselines; no numeric figures stated in the abstract.
not_tested: No per-item attribution of which memory entries caused a gain, and no reported comparison of how utility estimates behave under co-retrieval of multiple items; robustness of utility estimates across queries or tasks over time is not described.
axes: learned utility and reinforcement over memory
generalization and drift of item value
title: MemRL: Self-Evolving Agents via Runtime Reinforcement Learning on Episodic Memory

claim: Existing memory evaluations are static, and a streaming benchmark (Evo-Memory) plus a refine pipeline (ReMem) are needed to measure and achieve test-time learning with self-evolving memory across task streams.
method: Structure datasets into sequential task streams requiring search, adaptation and memory evolution after each interaction; unify and implement over ten memory modules; provide an ExpRAG baseline for experience retrieval and propose ReMem, an action-think-memory refine pipeline integrating reasoning, task actions and memory updates.
evidence: Over ten memory modules evaluated across 10 multi-turn goal-oriented and single-turn reasoning/QA datasets; ExpRAG baseline and ReMem pipeline proposed; no headline numbers stated in the abstract.
not_tested: No item-level scoring of individual memories (the benchmark measures task outcomes, not per-memory value), and no measurement of interference among co-retrieved experiences.
axes: measurement of per-item estimates
learned utility and reinforcement over memory
title: Evo-Memory: Benchmarking LLM Agent Test-time Learning with Self-Evolving Memory

claim: Parametric machine learning systems fail at latent learning (acquiring task-irrelevant information useful later), and episodic memory with retrieval can complement parametric learning to improve generalization.
method: Draw on cognitive science to link failures such as the reversal curse and agent navigation findings to absent latent learning, then show that a system with an oracle retrieval mechanism reuses learning experiences more flexibly, identifying components like within-example in-context learning as essential for using retrieved information.
evidence: Language modeling (reversal curse) and agent-based navigation settings; a system with oracle retrieval generalizes better across many of the tested challenges; no numeric headline figures stated in the abstract.
not_tested: Retrieval is oracle-based, so the value of a realistically retrieved item and the effect of noisy or conflicting retrieved sets are not tested; no learned utility or feedback-driven memory updates are examined.
axes: generalization and drift of item value
title: Latent learning: episodic memory complements parametric learning by enabling flexible reuse of experiences

claim: Retrieved skills are not oracular and can mislead in some states, so a credit-aware, on-policy bidirectional self-distillation (UCOB) that compares skill-conditioned and no-skill views at the same anchor state yields better skill utilization and evolution than fixed privileged-teacher assumptions.
method: Treat skill-conditioned and no-skill prompts as two on-policy context views of the same model, compare their return-to-go within the same task and anchor state, use the higher-return view as the local teacher, and use this local credit signal to drive skill memory updates, utility-aware retrieval and reflection self-training.
evidence: ALFWorld, WebShop and Search-QA across model scales; outperforms skill-free RL, skill-memory baselines and self-distillation methods, with up to 23.5 (ALFWorld) and 18.0 (WebShop) point gains over SOTA baselines; ablations, continual adaptation across environments and modest training overhead reported.
not_tested: Credit is assigned to the skill-conditioned prompt as a whole rather than to individual retrieved skills within a multi-skill set, and the noise or sample requirements of the per-skill utility estimates are not described.
axes: counterfactual attribution
learned utility and reinforcement over memory
generalization and drift of item value
title: UCOB: Learning to Utilize and Evolve Agentic Skills via Credit-Aware On-Policy Bidirectional Self-Distillation

claim: A dynamic procedural memory framework (ReMe) that distills, contextually reuses and utility-refines experiences beats passive append-only memory and shows a memory-scaling effect where a smaller model with memory outperforms a larger memoryless one.
method: Three mechanisms across the memory lifecycle: multi-faceted distillation (success patterns, failure triggers, comparative insights), context-adaptive reuse via scenario-aware indexing, and utility-based refinement that adds valid memories and prunes outdated ones.
evidence: BFCL-V3 and AppWorld; reported as new state-of-the-art among agent memory systems; Qwen3-8B with ReMe outperforms memoryless Qwen3-14B; code and the reme.library dataset released; no numeric scores stated in the abstract.
not_tested: How the utility signal used for pruning is estimated and whether pruning errs (removing items that were useful), and whether utility transfers when the query distribution or consumer model changes, are not described.
axes: learned utility and reinforcement over memory
generalization and drift of item value
title: Remember Me, Refine Me: A Dynamic Procedural Memory Framework for Experience-Driven Agent Evolution

claim: Agent memory is the critical substrate for self-evolving, long-horizon agents, and memory management is becoming a trainable capability that should be understood along substrate, cognitive mechanism and memory subject dimensions.
method: Survey organizing agent memory along three dimensions (substrate, cognitive mechanism, memory subject), analyzing memory operations under single- and multi-agent topologies, learning policies over memory operations, and reviewing benchmarks and metrics for memory utility.
evidence: Survey of hundreds of 2025 memory papers; no experiments or numbers.
not_tested: As a survey it reports no experiments; it does not test item-level credit assignment methods or compare per-item utility metrics empirically.
axes: learned utility and reinforcement over memory
measurement of per-item estimates
title: A Survey of Agent Memory in the Second Half: Towards Self-Evolving and Long-Horizon Agents

claim: Scoring replay-buffer transitions by a weighted combination of reward magnitude and TD error and evicting low-utility ones speeds learning and improves final returns over static retention schemes.
method: A DQN agent with an adaptive buffer that assigns each transition a utility from immediate reward magnitude and TD error, retains high-utility transitions and evicts low-utility ones under capacity pressure, with uniform sampling over the retained set and logs of utility and evictions.
evidence: CartPole-v1 and Acrobot-v1 with DQN; learns faster than FIFO and PER on CartPole-v1, higher final returns on Acrobot-v1; matches or slightly outperforms PER in final returns on CartPole-v1; baselines are Uniform Replay (FIFO), PER with FIFO eviction and Random Eviction, averaged over multiple seeds; no numeric figures stated.
not_tested: Only two small classic-control tasks are used, so transfer of utility scores to larger domains or LLM-agent memory is untested; the utility is a fixed heuristic, not a counterfactual estimate of a transition's effect on outcomes.
axes: learned utility and reinforcement over memory
generalization and drift of item value
title: Utility-Driven Selective Memory for Reinforcement Learning: A Biologically Inspired Replay Framework

claim: Early experience, interaction data from the agent's own actions where future states serve as supervision without rewards, is a practical bridge between imitation learning and fully experience-driven agents, improving effectiveness and out-of-domain generalization.
method: Two strategies for using early-experience data: implicit world modeling (using collected states to ground the policy in environment dynamics) and self-reflection (learning from suboptimal actions to improve reasoning), followed by evaluation as a foundation for subsequent RL.
evidence: Eight diverse environments and multiple model families; consistent improvements in effectiveness and out-of-domain generalization; in environments with verifiable rewards, early experience provides a strong foundation for subsequent RL; no numeric figures stated in the abstract.
not_tested: The paper trains on experience rather than retrieving it, so no per-item retrieval utility, attribution or set-level interference among retrieved items is examined.
title: Agent Learning via Early Experience

claim: Trajectory-indexed memory utilities disperse feedback over a growing state space and jointly assigned trajectory rewards contaminate co-retrieved memories (the memory-reward trap), and representing utility with a fixed-dimensional reduced-order per-task state concentrates feedback and limits persistent reward contamination.
method: RoMeRL represents the growing utility space with a fixed-dimensional per-task memory state factorized by outcome polarity and memory dynamics, incorporating new experiences through a fixed set of semantic coordinates whose contents are updated or replaced, with theory on average feedback per coordinate and steady-state occupancy of erroneous coordinates.
evidence: ALFWorld and LifelongAgentBench; improves task performance, reduces Cold-Q ratio by 80.0%, increases feedback density by about 6.0x, reduces maintained memory size by 84.4%, and cuts LLM calls by 21.1%.
not_tested: No direct counterfactual (leave-one-out) measurement of an individual memory's causal effect to validate that the utility coordinates track true item value, and the theory relies on a generic coordinate-transition model rather than measured transitions.
axes: learned utility and reinforcement over memory
set-level effects
measurement of per-item estimates
title: RoMeRL: Balancing Feedback Coverage and the Memory-Reward Trap in Self-Evolving Agent Memory via Reduced-Order Utility States

claim: Memory evolution in continual LLM agents is shaped by interactions among accumulated memories, with relationship-specific interference sharply suppressing update plasticity while benign accumulation has limited effect.
method: Controlled Memory Interference (CMI), a diagnostic and data-generation framework that constructs memories with controlled relationships (differing state, temporal validity, authority) and measures update plasticity and stability under lexical and dense retrieval, then uses the generated examples for interference-aware memory learning.
evidence: Controlled memory-evolution experiments with lexical and dense retrieval; interference blocks target-memory exposure or disrupts its downstream use; poisoning is more sensitive to update-authority cues than recency; CMI-generated examples improve distinction between valid updates and interfering memories while preserving original task performance; no numeric figures stated.
not_tested: Interference is studied under synthetic controlled relationships rather than naturally accumulated agent memories, and no learned per-item utility or feedback-based update is examined.
axes: set-level effects
generalization and drift of item value
title: Controlled Memory Interference in Continual LLM Agents

claim: Explicit preference memory distilled from purchase history into concise, query-independent signals is a practical and effective building block for personalized product reranking in LLM-based shopping agents.
method: MemRerank distills user purchase history into concise, query-independent preference signals via a memory extractor trained with reinforcement learning, using downstream reranking performance as supervision.
evidence: An end-to-end benchmark built around an LLM-based 1-in-5 product selection task; experiments with two LLM-based rerankers show MemRerank consistently outperforms no-memory, raw-history, and off-the-shelf memory baselines, with gains of up to +10.61 absolute points in 1-in-5 accuracy.
not_tested: Whether the gain can be attributed to individual distilled memory items rather than the memory as a whole; how the RL-trained extractor behaves as user preferences drift over time or across domains outside the benchmark.
axes: learned utility and reinforcement over memory
measurement of per-item estimates
title: MemRerank: Preference Memory for Personalized Product Reranking

claim: An agent's reliance on memory can be modeled as an explicit, user-controllable dimension, avoiding both memory anchoring and memory under-utilization in long-term interaction.
method: Introduces a behavioral metric of memory dependence quantifying the influence of past interactions on current outputs, then proposes SteeM, a Steerable Memory Agent that lets users dynamically regulate memory reliance from a fresh-start mode to a high-fidelity mode.
evidence: Experiments across different scenarios show the approach consistently outperforms conventional prompting and rigid memory masking strategies; specific models, benchmarks, and numbers are not stated in the abstract.
not_tested: Which specific memory items drive the anchoring effect (the dependence metric is aggregate rather than per-item); whether the memory-dependence metric agrees with counterfactual removal of individual memories.
axes: set-level effects
generalization and drift of item value
title: Controllable Memory Usage: Balancing Anchoring and Innovation in Long-Term Human-Agent Interaction

claim: A hybrid episodic-procedural memory that adaptively reuses partially overlapping successful experiences improves multi-turn tool-use policies at both inference and RL training time.
method: H-EPM builds a tool graph from accumulated trajectories whose edges capture recurring tool-to-tool dependencies augmented with compact episodic context summaries, balancing episodic recall and procedural execution at inference and biasing RL exploration toward historically successful tool transitions.
evidence: Multi-turn tool-use benchmarks; inference-time gains of up to fifty percent over strong baselines and RL policy gains of up to forty percent on out-of-distribution tasks; specific models are not stated in the abstract.
not_tested: Whether individual tool-graph edges or episodic summaries are credited or pruned based on their measured contribution to outcomes; how the memory behaves when past successful transitions become stale or misleading as the environment changes.
axes: learned utility and reinforcement over memory
generalization and drift of item value
title: Experience-Evolving Multi-Turn Tool-Use Agent with Hybrid Episodic-Procedural Memory

claim: Augmenting outcome rewards with local rewards derived from token-level attribution to the final answer resolves the fine-grained credit-assignment bottleneck in RL-based learning of memory-construction policies.
method: AttriMem trains a memory-construction policy (what to extract, store, update, compress, or discard) with RL, combining a global outcome reward with local process rewards computed from token-level contributions of memory contents to the final answer.
evidence: Long-horizon dialogue question answering; AttriMem outperforms retrieval-based, heuristic, and RL-based baselines, generalizes across benchmarks and answer models, and stabilizes RL optimization; headline numbers are not stated in the abstract.
not_tested: Whether token-level attribution scores agree with counterfactual removal of the attributed memory contents; how noisy the attribution-derived local rewards are and how many episodes are needed for them to be reliable.
axes: counterfactual attribution
learned utility and reinforcement over memory
measurement of per-item estimates
title: AttriMem: Attribution-Guided Process Feedback for Agent Memory Learning

claim: Agent-specific credit for a multi-agent memory pipeline can be derived from the final task reward alone, without task-specific annotations, by expanding the pipeline into a tree and Monte Carlo averaging over subsequent branches.
method: TreeMem extends the builder-summarizer-retrieval pipeline into a tree in which each agent's outputs branch into multiple continuations; each agent's contribution is estimated by Monte Carlo averaging of final rewards over its downstream branches, and all agent policies are updated simultaneously with these signals.
evidence: Long-horizon benchmarks; TreeMem improves memory system performance over strong baselines; specific models, benchmarks, and headline numbers are not stated in the abstract.
not_tested: Credit is assigned at the agent level rather than to individual memory items, so it does not test which stored memories helped; the cost of the branch rollouts and how many branches are needed for stable estimates are not stated.
axes: counterfactual attribution
learned utility and reinforcement over memory
measurement of per-item estimates
title: Tree-based Credit Assignment for Multi-Agent Memory System

claim: Propagating credit backward through a provenance DAG of memory dependencies with TD(λ) eligibility traces improves episodic-memory agents over methods that evaluate each memory in isolation.
method: MemQ records a provenance DAG of which memories were retrieved when each new memory was created, maintains Q-values per memory, and applies TD(λ) traces with credit decaying as (γλ)^d in DAG depth, formalized as an Exogenous-Context MDP.
evidence: Six benchmarks spanning OS interaction, function calling, code generation, multimodal reasoning, embodied reasoning, and expert-level QA; MemQ achieves the highest success rate on all six in generalization evaluation and runtime learning, with gains up to +5.7 pp on multi-step tasks and +0.77 pp on single-step classification.
not_tested: Whether the Q-values assigned to individual memories agree with counterfactual removal of those memories; how credit is split among co-retrieved memories at the same DAG level and whether Q-values remain valid as the task stream drifts.
axes: learned utility and reinforcement over memory
generalization and drift of item value
set-level effects
title: MemQ: Integrating Q-Learning into Self-Evolving Memory Agents over Provenance DAGs

claim: Decentralized retrieval of relevant trajectories as in-context memory, scored by a hybrid individual- and team-level utility, enables faster adaptation to unseen tasks in cooperative multi-agent RL.
method: MAICC trains a centralized embedding model of trajectories, distills it into decentralized approximations, retrieves relevant trajectories as context for each agent, balances test-time online data with offline memory, and scores memories with a hybrid utility combining individual and team returns for credit assignment across agents.
evidence: Cooperative MARL benchmarks Level-Based Foraging (LBF) and SMAC v1/v2; MAICC adapts faster to unseen tasks than existing methods; specific numbers are not stated in the abstract.
not_tested: Whether the hybrid utility score of a retrieved trajectory reflects its causal effect on the episode outcome; the paper credits agents rather than measuring the value of individual retrieved memories, and does not test interference among co-retrieved trajectories.
axes: learned utility and reinforcement over memory
generalization and drift of item value
title: Multi-agent In-context Coordination via Decentralized Memory Retrieval

claim: Memory usefulness changes across interaction stages, so multi-horizon retrieval with learned episode-level and turn-level policies improves experience reuse in interactive text-to-SQL agents.
method: MERIT maintains episode-level memory for global strategic guidance and turn-level memory for local decision support, learns both retrieval policies with RL, and uses a lightweight Process Reward Model to provide dense proxy rewards for turn-level memory selection.
evidence: BIRD-Interact: MERIT outperforms no-memory, static-retrieval, and dynamic-retrieval baselines in success rate while reducing average interaction turns; positive cross-benchmark transfer on Spider2-Snow without benchmark-specific tuning; headline numbers are not stated in the abstract.
not_tested: Whether the PRM's proxy rewards for a retrieved memory agree with its counterfactual contribution to task success; whether learned retrieval values remain stable as the memory store grows or becomes stale.
axes: learned utility and reinforcement over memory
generalization and drift of item value
measurement of per-item estimates
title: Learning to Retrieve: Dual-Level Long-Term Memory for Text-to-SQL Agents

claim: Agent memory systems have uncharacterized system-level behavior, and design choices shift cost between the write (construction) and read (retrieval, generation) paths in ways that yield actionable deployment recommendations.
method: Introduces a four-axis system-oriented taxonomy of agent memory systems, builds a phase-aware profiling harness attributing cost to construction, retrieval, and generation, and characterizes ten representative systems across two benchmark suites.
evidence: Ten representative agent memory systems profiled across two benchmark suites; yields 10 system recommendations on construction scheduling, capability floors, amortization via query volume, freshness-latency tradeoffs, and fleet-scale management; no headline accuracy numbers stated.
not_tested: It attributes cost, not task benefit, to memory phases, so it does not estimate the value of any stored or retrieved memory item; it does not examine how freshness or staleness of individual items affects downstream quality.
axes: generalization and drift of item value
title: Agent Memory: Characterization and System Implications of Stateful Long-Horizon Workloads

claim: A structured, evolving memory graph built from high-return experiences and amortized LLM outputs can shape advantage estimation to speed early sparse-reward RL learning while requiring substantially fewer online LLM queries and preserving convergence guarantees.
method: MIRA stores trajectory segments and subgoal structures in a memory graph, derives a utility signal from it that softly adjusts advantage estimation without modifying the reward, and decays the utility term as the policy surpasses the LLM-derived priors.
evidence: Sparse or delayed reward RL environments; MIRA outperforms RL baselines and achieves returns comparable to approaches relying on frequent LLM supervision while using substantially fewer online LLM queries; theoretical analysis shows utility-based shaping improves early-stage learning; specific environments and numbers are not stated in the abstract.
not_tested: Whether individual memory-graph entries are credited or pruned according to their measured effect on returns; how unreliable LLM-derived entries in the graph are detected and how their value degrades as the policy improves.
axes: learned utility and reinforcement over memory
generalization and drift of item value
title: MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance

claim: Augmenting online RL for mobile GUI agents with a hierarchical, self-evolving experience memory improves credit assignment in long-horizon tasks and enables cross-task and cross-application experience transfer, outperforming RL baselines and static reuse strategies.
method: UI-Mem stores workflows, subtask skills and failure patterns as parameterized templates in a Hierarchical Experience Memory, injects varying levels of memory guidance across trajectories in each rollout group via Stratified Group Sampling, and runs a Self-Evolving Loop that continuously abstracts new strategies and errors into memory.
evidence: Online GUI benchmarks for mobile agents; UI-Mem is reported to significantly outperform traditional RL baselines and static reuse strategies with strong generalization to unseen applications; no numeric headline figures given in the abstract.
not_tested: No attribution of outcome improvements to individual memory entries (which workflow or failure template helped or hurt a given rollout) and no measurement of whether stale or wrong templates accumulate in the self-evolving memory over time.
axes: learned utility and reinforcement over memory
generalization and drift of item value
title: UI-Mem: Self-Evolving Experience Memory for Online Reinforcement Learning in Mobile GUI Agents

claim: Integrating Hindsight Experience Replay into Multi-updates Option Critic, and augmenting goal relabeling with virtual goals from the agent's effector positions, makes option learning tractable in sparse-reward multi-goal environments including object manipulation.
method: MOC-HER relabels goals from achieved outcomes within MOC; 2HER adds virtual goals derived from effector positions so that both object interaction and task completion are rewarded in hindsight.
evidence: Robotic manipulation tasks; MOC-2HER achieves success rates up to 90% versus under 11% for MOC and MOC-HER.
not_tested: Not evaluated outside robotic manipulation or against non-option-based HER baselines (e.g. flat DDPG+HER) in the abstract; no analysis of which relabeled transitions in the replay buffer actually drive learning.
title: Enabling Option Learning in Sparse Rewards with Hindsight Experience Replay

claim: External memory does not eliminate the continual-learning stability-plasticity problem for LLM agents; it relocates it to retrieval, where old and new experiences compete under a limited context window, and memory representation and organization choices trade off forward transfer against forgetting.
method: A (k,v) framework disentangles how experience is represented from how it is organized for retrieval, applied in sequential-task experiments to compare memory designs.
evidence: Sequential-task experiments in ALFWorld and BabyAI; abstract procedural memories transfer more reliably than detailed trajectories, negative transfer disproportionately harms hard cases, and finer-grained organization can yield strong forward transfer while inducing severe forgetting; no numeric figures in the abstract.
not_tested: Item-level attribution of negative transfer to specific memories is not described, and the number of task sequences or models over which transfer/forgetting effects are estimated is not stated.
axes: set-level effects
generalization and drift of item value
title: When Continual Learning Moves to Memory: A Study of Experience Reuse in LLM Agents

claim: Agents consuming retrieved memory fall into a compliance trap: they adopt conflicting memory at the first exposed decision point even when it is task-wrong, repeated exposure amplifies the error, recovery is weak, and once agents comply their success collapses to a low floor so stronger agents suffer larger absolute damage.
method: The Entry-Propagation-Recovery (E-P-R) trajectory-level framework asks where memory first changes an action, whether the change carries forward, and whether the agent recovers, instantiated on WebArena and a purpose-built controlled benchmark, MemTrapBench.
evidence: WebArena and MemTrapBench across multiple models; conflicting memory induces similar compliance rates across models while success rates after compliance collapse to a low floor; no numeric figures in the abstract.
not_tested: Does not report whether the harm depends on the number or composition of co-retrieved (conflicting plus correct) entries, nor whether any consumption-aware control policy actually mitigates the trap.
axes: set-level effects
measurement of per-item estimates
title: The Compliance Trap: Diagnosing How AI Agents Consume Conflicting Memory

claim: Shapley-based attribution can be adapted to identify influential retrieved documents in RAG, and cheaper SHAP approximations can approximate exact attributions while reducing the number of costly LLM calls, including under inter-document redundancy, complementarity and synergy.
method: Systematically apply Shapley values at the RAG document level and compare exact Shapley against computationally tractable approximations and existing LLM attribution methods, evaluating attribution fidelity and explainability in identifying critical documents.
evidence: RAG document-level attribution setting; models, benchmarks and headline numbers not stated in the abstract.
not_tested: No stated evaluation of attribution stability across repeated LLM calls or of whether attributed document values transfer across queries; multi-step agent trajectories are not addressed.
axes: counterfactual attribution
set-level effects
measurement of per-item estimates
title: Source Attribution in Retrieval-Augmented Generation

claim: Treating memory admission as a structured decision over five interpretable factors gives transparent, efficient control of long-term memory and a better precision-recall tradeoff at lower latency than LLM-native memory systems.
method: A-MAC decomposes memory value into future utility, factual confidence, semantic novelty, temporal recency and content type prior, combines rule-based feature extraction with a single LLM-assisted utility assessment, and learns domain-adaptive admission policies via cross-validated optimization.
evidence: LoCoMo benchmark; F1 improved to 0.583 with 31% lower latency than state-of-the-art LLM-native memory systems; ablation identifies content type prior as the most influential factor.
not_tested: Whether the predicted future utility of admitted items matches their realized downstream utility is not reported, and admission is evaluated on one benchmark without post-admission feedback updating item value.
axes: learned utility and reinforcement over memory
generalization and drift of item value
title: Adaptive Memory Admission Control for LLM Agents

claim: Weighting memory entries by usage frequency, semantic relevance and an externally validated freshness signal, with conflict-triggered refresh, mitigates memory overload and temporal staleness in long-running agents.
method: MemCurrency assigns each memory a currency weight from usage frequency, semantic relevance and a freshness signal from validation against external sources, and a conflict-detection module triggers refresh when newly retrieved information contradicts stored entries.
evidence: 30-day continuous-interaction simulation adapted from RealTimeQA; 89.2% temporal information accuracy versus 73.5% standard RAG, 72.4% full-memory and 67.1% fixed-window baselines, with substantially less storage.
not_tested: No ablation isolating the contribution of usage-frequency decay versus the freshness signal, and no evaluation on interactive agent tasks beyond a QA simulation or with the external validation source unavailable or wrong.
axes: learned utility and reinforcement over memory
generalization and drift of item value
title: Memcurrency: Memory Decay and Refresh Mechanism for Long-Running LLM Agents

claim: Per-evidence-item operational utility in RAG can be measured by intervention, and answer-only evaluation misses important evidence effects, including non-additive interactions among multi-hop supports.
method: CUE-R perturbs individual evidence items with REMOVE, REPLACE and DUPLICATE operators and measures changes in correctness, proxy-based grounding faithfulness and confidence error plus a trace-divergence signal, with an evidence-role taxonomy for interpretation.
evidence: HotpotQA and 2WikiMultihopQA with Qwen-3 8B and GPT-5.2; REMOVE and REPLACE substantially harm correctness and grounding with large trace shifts, DUPLICATE is often answer-redundant but not behaviorally neutral, a zero-retrieval control confirms effects come from meaningful retrieval, and removing both multi-hop supports harms far more than either single removal.
not_tested: Single-shot RAG only, so no multi-step agent trajectories or persistent memory; the cost of the interventions and the variance of per-item estimates across repeated runs are not reported.
axes: counterfactual attribution
set-level effects
measurement of per-item estimates
title: CUE-R: Beyond the Final Answer in Retrieval-Augmented Generation

claim: Training agents with reinforcement learning to construct and update a complex memory system, rewarded by downstream QA accuracy, yields better memory construction than pre-defined memory instructions and generalizes far beyond training lengths.
method: Mem-alpha trains agents via RL on a specialized dataset of multi-turn interactions paired with evaluation questions; agents process sequential chunks, extract and store content into core, episodic and semantic memory components using multiple tools, with reward from downstream QA accuracy over the full history.
evidence: Significant improvements over existing memory-augmented agent baselines; trained on instances up to 30k tokens and generalizes to sequences over 400k tokens (13x training length); specific benchmarks and numbers not stated in the abstract.
not_tested: The reward is episode-level QA accuracy, so credit is not assigned to individual stored items; not tested on interactive task environments beyond QA.
axes: learned utility and reinforcement over memory
title: Mem-α: Learning Memory Construction via Reinforcement Learning

claim: Dynamically refining world-model reward estimates and uncertainty penalties with a dual-agent scheme improves offline RL recommendation policies over methods that treat learned rewards as static look-up tables.
method: DARLR uses a selector agent to pick reference users balancing similarity and diversity, the recommender aggregates their information to iteratively refine reward estimates for dynamic reward shaping, and the selected users' statistical features adapt an uncertainty penalty.
evidence: Four recommender benchmark datasets; superior performance over baselines reported, no numeric headline figures in the abstract.
not_tested: Not concerned with retrieved memory or LLM agents; no evaluation with online users or of the robustness of the selected reference-user set.
title: DARLR: Dual-Agent Offline Reinforcement Learning for Recommender Systems with Dynamic Reward

claim: Gating memory restructuring with a reward-prediction-error critic (Fast/Slow routing) lets an LLM agent maintain lifelong memory at far lower token and write-latency cost while matching or beating append-and-evolve systems such as A-MEM.
method: A lightweight Critic Router scores each input for Surprise and Utility (RPE); routine low-RPE inputs are bypassed or cached in an O(1) fast buffer, while high-RPE inputs such as factual contradictions or preference shifts trigger a 'dopamine' signal that runs the O(N) memory-evolution pipeline to reshape the agent's knowledge graph.
evidence: LoCoMo-Noise, a new benchmark that injects controlled conversational noise into long-term sessions; reports over 80% reduction in token consumption, elimination of the O(N^2) write bottleneck, and better multi-hop reasoning and adversarial resilience than baselines; no accuracy figures or model names given in the abstract.
not_tested: Whether the critic's write-time Surprise/Utility score predicts the downstream benefit of a stored item (no per-item counterfactual check); the cost of false negatives, i.e. low-RPE inputs that are bypassed but later needed.
axes: learned utility and reinforcement over memory
generalization and drift of item value
title: D-MEM: Dopamine-Gated Agentic Memory via Reward Prediction Error Routing

claim: Dynamically refining preference memory by fusing sliding-window averages with exponential moving averages improves LLM output quality in long-term conversations compared with memory systems that only store and retrieve.
method: PAMU constructs a fused preference-aware representation that combines sliding-window averages (short-term fluctuations) with exponential moving averages (long-term tendencies) and updates it as user behavior and context evolve.
evidence: Five task scenarios of the LoCoMo dataset, applied on top of five baselines; reports 'significant' improvements in output quality; no numbers or model names in the abstract.
not_tested: Whether gains come from tracking preference drift versus simply smoothing noisy preferences; no attribution of which stored preferences drove the improvement; sensitivity to window size and EMA decay hyperparameters.
axes: generalization and drift of item value
learned utility and reinforcement over memory
title: Preference-Aware Memory Update for Long-Term LLM Agents

claim: Existing long-term memory benchmarks reduce to fact retrieval; when memory consolidation and frequent knowledge updates are tested, current LLMs and memory agents frequently reuse invalidated memories and fail to reconcile evolving ones, with memory agents offering only marginal improvements.
method: Introduce Memora, a benchmark of weeks-to-months-long user conversations with three memory-grounded tasks (remembering, reasoning, recommending), validated by automated memory-grounding checks and human evaluation, plus Forgetting-Aware Memory Accuracy (FAMA), a metric that penalizes reliance on obsolete or invalidated memory.
evidence: Four LLMs and six memory agents evaluated on Memora; findings are frequent reuse of invalid memories, failure to reconcile evolving memories, and marginal gains from memory agents; no numeric results in the abstract.
not_tested: Failures are not attributed to specific retrieved items and no per-item value is measured; the benchmark does not test whether agents can learn item utility from feedback over time.
axes: generalization and drift of item value
measurement of per-item estimates
title: From Recall to Forgetting: Benchmarking Long-Term Memory for Personalized Agents

claim: A retrieved document's value can be quantified as the change in the LLM's generation confidence with versus without it (Document Information Gain), and a reranker trained on DIG scores substantially improves RAG answer accuracy by filtering irrelevant or misleading documents.
method: Compute DIG per document as the difference in the LLM's confidence in the correct answer with and without that document augmented; train a specialized reranker on DIG scores to both distinguish and sort documents; filter and select the most valuable ones for generation.
evidence: Multiple models and QA benchmarks, single- and multi-retriever settings; on NaturalQA, exact-match gains of 17.9%, 4.5% and 12.5% over naive RAG, self-reflective RAG and ranking-based RAG; average 15.3% improvement with GPT-4o across all datasets.
not_tested: DIG is computed one document at a time, so interactions among co-retrieved documents (redundancy, conflict, ordering) are not captured; whether DIG scores transfer across generator models or query distributions is not examined.
axes: counterfactual attribution
measurement of per-item estimates
title: InfoGain-RAG: Boosting Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Document Information Gain-based Reranking and Filtering

claim: Credit for memory-writing actions in long-horizon agents is causally entangled with downstream tool failures, noisy observations and reasoning errors, and a hindsight-informed memory-specific advantage disentangles it, improving both task performance and attribution fidelity.
method: HiMPO estimates a memory update's local utility as the difference in task-relevant information recoverable from the previous versus updated memory under the same pre-write state, attenuates that credit with a bounded hindsight-relevance filter when the target outcome does not support it, and applies the resulting memory-specific advantage only to memory tokens while trajectory-level rewards train the rest of the policy.
evidence: Judge-based open-domain tasks and objective compressive-memory QA; improves over strong memory-based and RL-based baselines while preserving compressed-context efficiency; controlled interventions show reduced blame leakage from tool-induced errors and improved attribution fidelity; no numbers or model names in the abstract.
not_tested: Credit is assigned to memory-write actions, not to individual retrieved items, so the value of stored content at retrieval time is not estimated; the noise and sample cost of the local-utility estimator (how many episodes it needs) are not reported.
axes: counterfactual attribution
learned utility and reinforcement over memory
measurement of per-item estimates
title: HiMPO: Hindsight-Informed Memory Policy Optimization for Less-Entangled Credit in Long-Horizon Agents

claim: Truncated step-level sampling (trajectories sharing a prefix and differing only at the next step) combined with dense LLM-as-judge rewards for each reasoning step, search query and answer yields lower-variance, better-targeted policy gradients than sparse-outcome or heuristic process-reward RL for search-augmented reasoning.
method: SLATE generates k trajectories per example that share a common prefix and branch only at the next step, scores each reasoning step, search query and answer with a capable LLM judge, and proves that truncated sampling reduces advantage-estimate variance by up to a factor of T for T-step trajectories.
evidence: Seven QA benchmarks; SLATE consistently outperforms sparse-reward (Search-R1) and process-reward (StepSearch) baselines, with the largest gains on harder multi-hop tasks and smaller models; no specific numbers in the abstract.
not_tested: Credit is assigned to reasoning and query steps, not to individual retrieved documents; the reliability of the LLM judge's rewards and its compute cost per training step are not quantified.
axes: counterfactual attribution
measurement of per-item estimates
title: Truncated Step-Level Sampling with Process Rewards for Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning

claim: Retrieved memories can harm agents by inducing sycophancy (over-aligning with the user at the cost of factual accuracy or objective reasoning), and existing memory benchmarks miss this because they test storage, retrieval and updating rather than how retrieved memory influences downstream reasoning.
method: Build MemSyco-Bench with five tasks that test whether agents reject memory as factual evidence, respect memory's applicable scope, resolve conflicts between memory and objective evidence, track memory updates, and use valid memory for personalization.
evidence: Benchmark and resources released at github.com/XMUDeepLIT/MemSyco-Bench; the abstract reports no models, numbers or empirical findings.
not_tested: No results appear in the abstract, so whether any agent or memory system mitigates memory-induced sycophancy is unknown; the benchmark scores decisions, not the value of individual memory items.
axes: set-level effects
generalization and drift of item value
title: MemSyco-Bench: Benchmarking Sycophancy in Agent Memory

claim: When adapting a dual-encoder retriever with RL from reward-model feedback under a frozen document index, applying gradient updates only to retrieved items with positive advantage avoids the embedding-geometry degradation caused by pushing away negatives and outperforms standard RL and distillation.
method: PAO (Positive-Advantage-Only) computes advantages for retrieved items from reward-model feedback and applies policy-gradient updates only for positive-advantage items, pulling query embeddings toward high-reward regions while preserving global topological stability of the frozen index.
evidence: A massive industrial e-commerce dataset and public benchmarks; PAO 'significantly outperforms' standard RL and distillation baselines; no numbers in the abstract.
not_tested: Whether the per-item advantage from the reranker reflects true downstream utility rather than reranker preference; whether ignoring negative-advantage items lets harmful retrieved items persist; not tested with LLM generation or agent memory.
axes: learned utility and reinforcement over memory
title: Learning from What You Retrieve: Online RL Fine-Tuning for Semantic Retrieval

claim: Frozen, replaceable LLM executors can improve without parameter updates by reusing skills and failure lessons stored in a self-evolving experience graph retrieved through graph diffusion and utility-aware ranking.
method: Summarize historical trajectories into reusable skills and failure lessons as graph nodes, retrieve via graph diffusion and utility-aware ranking, train a lightweight retrieval copilot with RL using feedback that compares executor performance with and without retrieved experiences, and update the graph online from downstream task outcomes.
evidence: ExpSuite (question answering, math reasoning, code generation, ALFWorld, AppWorld); over the strongest baseline +12.2% and +4.7% on static tasks with smaller and larger executors, +21.4% and +12.7% in agentic environments, with 12.7% and 21.6% fewer interaction steps; ablations credit graph structure, utility-aware ranking and adaptive retrieval jointly.
not_tested: The with-versus-without feedback is at the level of the whole retrieved set, so credit is not attributed to individual experiences within it; whether utility estimates learned under one executor transfer to a replaced executor is not isolated from the overall model-agnosticism claim.
axes: counterfactual attribution
learned utility and reinforcement over memory
generalization and drift of item value
title: ExpGraph: Model-Agnostic Experience Learning with Graph-Structured Memory for LLM Agents

claim: RL search agents suffer retrieval-equivalence collapse (distinct query strings yield increasingly overlapping evidence sets, leaving within-group returns with little retrieval contrast), and reformulating retrieval as finite action selection over a menu of evidence plus structured non-myopic credit fixes this and improves QA.
method: Harness-G has the environment construct a menu of evidence sentences and entities, track retrieval state and validate each choice while the policy selects an item or answers; Structured Non-myopic Credit (SNC) uses a frozen answer scorer to compare the selected action with its same-state alternatives and assigns downstream gains back to the earlier actions that enabled them.
evidence: Six QA benchmarks at 1.5B and 3B scales; highest average F1 at both scales, beating the strongest baseline Graph-R1 by 10.74 points at 1.5B and 3.98 at 3B; retrieval aliasing observed during Search-R1 training.
not_tested: Stability of SNC's per-action credit across seeds and the number of rollouts it needs; only small models and QA, no agentic-memory settings; whether environment-side menu construction biases which evidence is available for selection.
axes: counterfactual attribution
set-level effects
measurement of per-item estimates
title: Harness-G: A Graph-Structured Harness for Search Agents

claim: An adaptive budgeted forgetting framework that scores memories by recency, frequency and semantic alignment preserves long-horizon reasoning performance while preventing unbounded memory growth and reducing false memory behavior.
method: Regulate agent memory through relevance-guided scoring (recency, frequency, semantic alignment) under a bounded optimization budget so the memory stays stable within a constrained context.
evidence: Long-horizon conversational settings; motivated by LOCOMO/LOCCO degradation from 0.455 to 0.05 across stages and MultiWOZ at 78.2% accuracy with 6.8% false memory rate under persistent retention; comparative analysis reports long-horizon F1 improved beyond a 0.583 baseline, higher retention consistency and reduced false memory without increased context usage; models not named in the abstract.
not_tested: No causal check of whether an individual pruned or retained item actually changed an episode's outcome; no report of how sensitive results are to the scoring weights or to the false-memory measurement beyond the aggregate rate.
axes: generalization and drift of item value
title: Novel Memory Forgetting Techniques for Autonomous AI Agents: Balancing Relevance and Efficiency

claim: Retrieval alone does not make a memory valid evidence for the current query, and restoring each fragment's original episodic context (time, session span, participants) and checking it against query-implied conditions consistently improves long-term memory performance.
method: A four-stage pipeline: anchor each memory in its original episodic conditions, induce the evidence conditions implied by the query, retrieve with validity-aware prioritization (content-relevant items kept as fallback), and synthesize with the selected memories' structured context preserved for the generator.
evidence: Long-term memory benchmarks with several LLM backbones (not named in the abstract); RaMem reported to improve over strong memory baselines with average F1 gains of more than 10%.
not_tested: No ablation showing how much of the gain comes from excluding context-incompatible items versus the synthesis stage; no measurement of how often validity-aware retrieval wrongly demotes a memory that was in fact the correct evidence.
axes: set-level effects
generalization and drift of item value
title: RaMem: Contextual Reinstatement for Long-term Agentic Memory

claim: Current memory-augmented agents perform poorly in long-horizon settings where information is repeatedly updated and interferes across memories, especially on questions requiring aggregation over multiple pieces of evidence, with accuracy degrading as intervening updates increase.
method: Build MINTEval, a benchmark of long, interconnected, frequently updated contexts across four domains (state tracking, multi-turn dialogue, Wikipedia revisions, GitHub commits) with single-target recall and multi-target aggregation questions, and evaluate representative memory systems on it.
evidence: 15.6k QA pairs over contexts averaging 138.8k tokens and up to 1.8M tokens; 7 systems (vanilla long-context LLMs, RAG, memory-augmented agent frameworks) evaluated; average accuracy 27.9%; performance attributed mainly to retrieval and memory construction; accuracy degrades with the number of intervening updates.
not_tested: No scoring of individual memory items (only question-level accuracy), so which stored item caused a failure is not attributed; no evaluation of methods designed to handle updates, only of existing systems.
axes: set-level effects
measurement of per-item estimates
title: MINTEval: Evaluating Memory under Multi-Target Interference in Long-Horizon Agent Systems

claim: An ACT-R-inspired activation mechanism with temporal decay, semantic similarity and probabilistic noise lets an LLM dialogue agent retrieve and forget memories in a human-like, context-sensitive way.
method: Integrate ACT-R with an LLM dialogue agent using vector-based activation combining temporal decay, semantic similarity and stochastic noise to decide which memories are retrieved or forgotten based on context, time and usage frequency.
evidence: Simulation experiments with a dialogue agent; reported reproduction of memory reinforcement through repeated topics and stochastic variability in retrieval; identified parameters balancing contextual sensitivity and memory stability; no task benchmark or numeric accuracy stated.
not_tested: No measurement of whether the human-like forgetting improves task outcomes or answer quality; no comparison against non-decaying retrieval baselines on an external benchmark.
axes: learned utility and reinforcement over memory
generalization and drift of item value
title: Human-Like Remembering and Forgetting in LLM Agents: An ACT-R-Inspired Memory Architecture

claim: Rewarding a chunk-wise memory agent by how much its final memory raises the per-token log-likelihood of the ground-truth answer, applied only on successful trajectories and normalized, improves RL training over sparse or lexical intermediate rewards.
method: InfoMem computes an answer-conditioned information-gain reward on the final memory, restricts it to successful trajectories, normalizes it before reward composition, and trains under GRPO with the same budget as baselines.
evidence: Long-context memory-agent tasks trained with GRPO; InfoMem improves over comparable memory-agent RL baselines; analyses indicate the reward should apply to successful trajectories, be normalized, and be answer- rather than query-conditioned; specific models and benchmark numbers not given in the abstract.
not_tested: Reward operates on the whole final memory, so credit to individual memory updates or chunks is not attributed; robustness of the log-likelihood signal when the reference answer is one of several valid phrasings is not examined.
axes: learned utility and reinforcement over memory
measurement of per-item estimates
title: InfoMem: Training Long-Context Memory Agents with Answer-Conditioned Information Gain

claim: Retrieving experiences at each decision step conditioned on the current observation, with a self-evolving experience library and step-level credit assignment, outperforms RL baselines on multi-turn agent tasks where one-shot static retrieval becomes mismatched.
method: Cluster step-level observations for cluster-indexed retrieval, maintain an experience library that admits distilled successes and failure patterns via score-based admission and rate-limited extraction, and optimize the policy with step-level advantage estimation.
evidence: Long-horizon multi-turn agent benchmarks (not named in the abstract); SLEA-RL reported superior to various RL baselines; no headline numbers stated.
not_tested: The step-level credit assignment targets policy actions, and the abstract gives no evidence that credit is propagated back to the retrieved experience items themselves; the effect of score-based admission thresholds on library quality is not reported.
axes: learned utility and reinforcement over memory
generalization and drift of item value
title: SLEA-RL: Step-Level Experience Augmented Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Turn Agentic Training

claim: Treating memory as a control problem, deciding when to retrieve based on uncertainty and buffer utility and what to reinforce based on contribution to the response, with decay-driven accessibility rather than deletion, sustains long-horizon performance at lower token cost.
method: Oblivion separates a read path (consult memory only when agent uncertainty and memory-buffer utility warrant it) from a write path (strengthen memories that contributed to forming the response), with decay reducing accessibility over time and enabling hierarchical organization of persistent strategies and on-demand details.
evidence: Static and dynamic long-horizon interaction benchmarks (not named in the abstract); Oblivion outperforms direct and memory-augmented baselines and reduces token cost by up to 73% at 120K interaction spans.
not_tested: How the write path determines that a memory contributed to the response is not described, so whether reinforcement correctly credits the responsible item versus co-retrieved items is untested; no ablation isolating the decay schedule from the read-gating.
axes: learned utility and reinforcement over memory
generalization and drift of item value
title: Oblivion: Self-Adaptive Agentic Memory Control through Decay-Driven Activation

claim: Few-shot inverse RL on a new task with substantial variations succeeds when the reward is decomposed into a multitask discriminator that transfers shared structure from related tasks and a proximity function that guides the agent back toward expert behavior.
method: MPG learns two reward components, a generalizable discriminator trained across related-task demonstrations and a proximity function measuring deviation from expert states, and uses them jointly with online agent experience for few-shot IRL.
evidence: Multiple navigation and manipulation tasks under variations in object configurations, table layouts and initial robot poses; average success rate 81.2%, outperforming the strongest per-task baseline by 24.7 percentage points on average.
not_tested: No evaluation with LLM agents or retrieved memories; transfer is tested across related robotic tasks only, and how the method degrades when related-task demonstrations are dissimilar is not reported.
title: Generalize and Guide: Decomposing Rewards for Few-Shot Inverse Reinforcement Learning

claim: Replaying retrieved experiences verbatim causes negative transfer, and training a policy to critique and reconstruct retrieved experience conditioned on the current state substantially improves performance and OOD robustness.
method: At each decision step a single policy model critiques and rewrites the retrieved experience into context-grounded guidance before acting, with the reconstruction behavior learned end-to-end via GRPO.
evidence: ALFWorld and WebShop; MemHarness substantially outperforms pure RL and static memory-augmented baselines with strong OOD robustness; analyses indicate reconstruction also acts as latent guidance during training; no numeric results in the abstract.
not_tested: Whether reconstruction helps or hurts when the retrieved experience is actually wrong or irrelevant is not separated from the case where it is merely mismatched; no attribution of gains to specific retrieved items versus the improved intrinsic reasoning.
axes: generalization and drift of item value
title: MemHarness: Memory Is Reconstructed, Not Replayed

claim: Stacking more scaffolding components onto an LLM agent is often worse than a task-specific subset because components interfere destructively, and greedy component selection is unreliable due to widespread submodularity violations.
method: A full 2^5 factorial experiment over five components (planning, tools, memory, self-reflection, retrieval) with main-effects regression and exact Shapley values to quantify individual contributions and interactions.
evidence: HotpotQA and GSM8K with Llama-3.1-8B/70B, 96 conditions, up to 10 seeds; single-tool agent beats All-In on HotpotQA (F1 0.233 vs 0.177, p=0.023); 3-component subset beats All-In on GSM8K (0.43 vs 0.24, p=0.010); regression R^2=0.916 (LOOCV 0.872); 183/325 (56.3%) submodularity violations; exploratory three-body synergy INT_3=+0.175, 95% CI [+0.003,+0.351]; replicates on Qwen2.5 and under prompt paraphrasing.
stated_limitations: A three-body synergy among Tool Use, Self-Reflection, and Retrieval is reported as exploratory.
not_tested: Shapley attribution is at the component level, not for individual retrieved or stored memory items; only two benchmarks and one primary model family are used, so the task-dependence of k* is not tested broadly.
axes: counterfactual attribution
set-level effects
title: More Is Not Always Better: Cross-Component Interference in LLM Agent Scaffolding

claim: Jointly meta-evolving an agent's experiential knowledge and its memory architecture (rather than fixing the architecture by hand) yields substantial performance gains and memory designs that transfer across tasks and backbone LLMs.
method: MemEvolve, a meta-evolutionary framework that evolves both stored experience and the memory architecture, built on EvolveLab, a codebase that distills twelve memory systems into a modular encode/store/retrieve/manage design space and serves as a standardized experimental arena.
evidence: Four agentic benchmarks; frameworks such as SmolAgent and Flash-Searcher improved by up to 17.06%; claimed cross-task and cross-LLM generalization of evolved memory architectures (specific benchmarks, models and other numbers not stated in the abstract).
not_tested: No per-item or per-component attribution of gains to specific evolved memory modules or stored experiences; no analysis of stability or drift of the evolved architecture over longer horizons or under noisy feedback.
axes: generalization and drift of item value
title: MemEvolve: Meta-Evolution of Agent Memory Systems

claim: Modeling memory-unit importance as a dynamic utility signal updated from usage, redundancy and temporal cues, and using it to strategically forget, improves long-context multi-step reasoning over static retrieval and heuristic decay.
method: SF-AMS: a utility-driven survival mechanism that updates each memory unit's importance from usage redundancy and temporal signals, inducing a hierarchical structure favoring stable entity-consistent information, plus Composite Importance Scoring combining semantic and entity-level signals for retrieval.
evidence: LoCoMo and LongMemEval-s; baselines LightMem, Mem0 (MemO) and A-Mem; +9.65 F1 on multi-hop reasoning with Qwen2.5-7B, +6.91 F1 on temporal reasoning with GPT-4o-mini, +6.53 F1 on open-domain tasks over the strongest baseline.
not_tested: Whether the utility scores are causally correct at the item level (no counterfactual or ablation check that forgotten units were actually harmless); robustness of the forgetting rule when usage signals are noisy or when frequently used but wrong items get reinforced.
axes: learned utility and reinforcement over memory
generalization and drift of item value
title: SF-AMS: Strategic Forgetting for Structured Memory in LLM Agent

claim: Agent memory is best understood as a write-manage-read loop coupled to perception and action, and current evaluation is shifting from static recall benchmarks to multi-session agentic tests that expose persistent gaps in existing systems.
method: A survey (2022 to early 2026) that formalizes agent memory, introduces a three-dimensional taxonomy (temporal scope, representational substrate, control policy), examines five mechanism families, analyzes four recent benchmarks, surveys applications and engineering concerns, and lists open challenges.
evidence: Survey; no experiments or headline numbers; covers five mechanism families (context-resident compression, retrieval-augmented stores, reflective self-improvement, hierarchical virtual context, policy-learned management) and four recent multi-session benchmarks.
not_tested: No empirical comparison of the surveyed mechanisms; open challenges such as causally grounded retrieval and learned forgetting are named but not operationalized or measured.
axes: learned utility and reinforcement over memory
measurement of per-item estimates
title: Memory for Autonomous LLM Agents:Mechanisms, Evaluation, and Emerging Frontiers

claim: An agent can be trained, via slow-fast co-evolution with on-policy self-distillation using outcome-calibrated memory attribution and privileged hindsight, to internalize selecting, using, writing and maintaining experience, outperforming memory systems and training-based methods.
method: OPD-Evolver: a fast loop where the agent reads, uses, writes and maintains a four-level memory hierarchy at test time, and a slow loop where outcome-calibrated memory attribution and privileged hindsight distill these abilities into the deployable policy.
evidence: Multi-domain benchmarks; surpasses ReasoningBank by up to 11.5% and Skill0 by about 5.8%; OPD-Evolver-9B reported as competitive with Qwen3.5-397B-A17B and Step-3.5-Flash (specific benchmarks not named in the abstract).
not_tested: Accuracy of the outcome-calibrated memory attribution itself is not validated against counterfactual re-runs; no report on whether the distilled policy's memory-management behavior degrades or drifts as the repository grows.
axes: counterfactual attribution
learned utility and reinforcement over memory
title: OPD-Evolver: Cultivating Holistic Agent Evolver via On-Policy Distillation

claim: Agent memory research has become fragmented and is better organized through the unified lenses of forms (token-level, parametric, latent), functions (factual, experiential, working) and dynamics (formation, evolution, retrieval), with memory treated as a first-class primitive.
method: A survey that delineates agent memory from LLM memory, RAG and context engineering, proposes taxonomies along forms, functions and dynamics, compiles benchmarks and open-source frameworks, and outlines frontiers including memory automation, RL integration, multimodal and multi-agent memory, and trustworthiness.
evidence: Survey; no experiments or headline numbers; a compiled summary of memory benchmarks and open-source frameworks.
not_tested: No empirical evaluation of any taxonomy category; RL integration is named as a frontier without analysis of credit-assignment failure modes.
axes: learned utility and reinforcement over memory
title: Memory in the Age of AI Agents

claim: No single agent-memory architecture dominates across workloads; effectiveness depends on aligning memory structure with the workload bottleneck, and localized maintenance is more cost-efficient than global reorganization.
method: An analytical framework decomposing agent memory into representation/storage, extraction, retrieval/routing and maintenance modules, with end-to-end evaluation, fine-grained module ablations and cost-performance analysis under realistic workloads.
evidence: 12 memory systems and two reference baselines across five benchmark workloads spanning 11 datasets; ablations quantify effects on representation fidelity, retrieval precision, update correctness and long-horizon stability; code released (no specific numbers in the abstract).
not_tested: Ablations are at the module level, not the individual-memory-item level; no measurement of how the retrieved set (order, conflicts, redundancy) affects outcomes.
axes: generalization and drift of item value
measurement of per-item estimates
title: Are We Ready For An Agent-Native Memory System?

claim: Agents that appear near-saturated on long-context memory benchmarks like LoCoMo perform poorly when memorization and action are coupled across interdependent multi-session tasks, exposing a gap in current memory evaluation.
method: MemoryArena, an evaluation gym of human-crafted agentic tasks with explicitly interdependent subtasks in multi-session Memory-Agent-Environment loops, spanning web navigation, preference-constrained planning, progressive information search and sequential formal reasoning.
evidence: Benchmark spanning four task families; agents with near-saturated LoCoMo performance perform poorly in the agentic setting (no specific numbers or models in the abstract).
not_tested: Scores are end-to-end task outcomes; the benchmark does not score individual stored memories or attribute later-session success to specific items.
axes: measurement of per-item estimates
title: MemoryArena: Benchmarking Agent Memory in Interdependent Multi-Session Agentic Tasks

claim: Memory agents require four core competencies (accurate retrieval, test-time learning, long-range understanding, conflict resolution) and current methods fail to master all four.
method: MemoryAgentBench, a benchmark combining reformulated existing datasets with newly constructed ones in an incremental multi-turn interactive setting, used to evaluate memory agents from context-based and RAG systems to agents with external memory modules and tools.
evidence: Diverse set of memory agents evaluated on the four competencies; results show no method masters all four (no headline numbers in the abstract).
not_tested: Conflict resolution is measured only as task outcome, not as which retrieved items were correctly favored or suppressed; no item-level scoring of memory quality.
axes: set-level effects
measurement of per-item estimates
title: Evaluating Memory in LLM Agents via Incremental Multi-Turn Interactions

claim: Precise cognitive-science-inspired definitions of RL agent memory types and a standardized evaluation methodology are needed because loosely defined memory concepts lead to erroneous judgments about agents' memory capabilities.
method: Defines memory types (long-term vs short-term, declarative vs procedural), categorizes classes of agent memory, proposes an experimental methodology for evaluating RL agent memory, and runs experiments showing what violating the methodology leads to.
evidence: Experiments with different RL agents demonstrating the consequences of not following the proposed methodology (no specific environments or numbers in the abstract).
not_tested: Concerns classical RL agents, not LLM agents with external retrieved memory; no evaluation of the value of individual stored items.
axes: measurement of per-item estimates
title:
Unraveling the Complexity of Memory in RL Agents: an Approach for
  Classification and Evaluation

claim: An LLM agent with a long-term experience memory updated by reinforcement learning (RLEM) can learn from successes and failures across episodes and task goals without fine-tuning, forming a semi-parametric RL agent that beats prior SOTA.
method: REMEMBERER equips the LLM with a long-term experience memory and uses Reinforcement Learning with Experience Memory (RLEM) to update the memory from episode outcomes.
evidence: Two RL task sets; average success rate over different initializations and training sets exceeds prior SOTA by 4% and 2%.
not_tested: Whether the RL updates correctly credit individual stored experiences versus co-retrieved ones is not examined; no analysis of value drift or staleness of stored experiences over long runs.
axes: learned utility and reinforcement over memory
title: Large Language Models Are Semi-Parametric Reinforcement Learning Agents
